questions.question: A client with severe asthma had loud wheezing but is now drowsy with minimal air movement and one-word speech. How should the RN interpret this change?
choices: Impending respiratory failure from worsening obstruction and fatigue
Improvement because wheezing is quieter
Expected sleepiness after exertion
A reason to stop respiratory monitoring
questions.explanation: A silent or nearly silent chest, drowsiness, poor speech, and fatigue indicate critically reduced airflow and require immediate airway support.

questions.question: A client with COPD exacerbation is hypoxemic. Which oxygen approach is safest?
choices: Give controlled oxygen promptly to the individualized target and reassess ventilation and blood gases when indicated
Withhold oxygen because all COPD clients retain carbon dioxide
Apply an arbitrary maximum flow without reassessment
Use pulse oximetry alone to determine carbon dioxide level
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia must be treated. Controlled titration and ventilation assessment reduce both oxygen deprivation and excessive-oxygen risks.

questions.question: Which feature most strongly supports asthma rather than COPD?
choices: Symptoms and expiratory airflow limitation that vary over time and improve between episodes
Persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction with long exposure history
Progressive daily sputum and fixed activity limitation
Emphysematous alveolar destruction
questions.explanation: Asthma characteristically varies over time and intensity, whereas COPD involves persistent airflow obstruction, though overlap can occur.

questions.question: Why is a short-acting beta agonist alone not an adequate long-term asthma strategy for adults and adolescents?
choices: It relieves bronchospasm but does not treat the underlying airway inflammation
It permanently cures airway inflammation
It replaces every controller medication
It prevents all future exacerbations without an inhaled corticosteroid
questions.explanation: Current asthma strategy uses inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment because bronchodilation alone does not address inflammation or exacerbation risk.

questions.question: Which finding best indicates improvement after treatment of an acute obstructive exacerbation?
choices: Easier speech, less work of breathing, stronger bilateral air entry, and improving oxygenation
Quieter wheezing with increasing drowsiness
Falling respiratory effort with worsening carbon dioxide retention
New hypotension and absent breath sounds on one side
questions.explanation: Improvement is judged by function, air entry, effort, mentation, and gas exchange—not wheeze volume alone.

questions.question: Which client is the best candidate for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation during a COPD exacerbation?
choices: An alert, cooperative client with hypercapnic respiratory distress who can protect the airway and manage secretions
An unresponsive client who is vomiting and cannot protect the airway
A client with severe facial trauma preventing mask seal
A client in respiratory arrest
questions.explanation: NIV can support selected cooperative clients with acute hypercapnic failure. Airway inability, vomiting, arrest, or severe mask barriers require another approach.

questions.question: Which instruction is correct for a typical dry-powder inhaler?
choices: Exhale away from the device, then inhale the dose quickly and deeply without exhaling into it
Inhale very slowly while pressing a propellant canister
Shake every dry-powder device vigorously after loading
Breathe moist air into the mouthpiece before each dose
questions.explanation: Dry-powder inhalers commonly require a forceful deep inhalation and protection from moisture. Device-specific instructions always take priority.

questions.question: How should the RN best evaluate whether a client can use a newly prescribed inhaler?
choices: Ask the client to perform a return demonstration with the exact device
Ask only whether the printed instructions were read
Assume all inhalers work the same way
Assess technique only after the next hospitalization
questions.explanation: Devices require different preparation and inhalation patterns. Return demonstration exposes errors that verbal agreement does not.

questions.question: A client with COPD suddenly develops unilateral absent breath sounds, pleuritic pain, severe dyspnea, and hypotension. Which complication requires immediate evaluation?
choices: Tension pneumothorax
Stable chronic bronchitis
Expected pursed-lip breathing
Routine inhaler side effect
questions.explanation: Sudden unilateral breath-sound loss with shock and respiratory distress is a life-threatening pneumothorax pattern.

questions.question: Which discharge plan best reduces future exacerbation risk?
choices: A written action plan, medication reconciliation, inhaler return demonstration, trigger and smoking support, vaccination review, and follow-up
A rescue inhaler without technique teaching or controller review
Instructions to avoid all physical activity permanently
A plan to seek help only after loss of consciousness
questions.explanation: Prevention combines correct therapy and technique, risk reduction, clear escalation steps, and timely follow-up.
